summary: Meta, via a blog post by global head of Safety Antigone Davis, is backing federal legislation requiring parental approval for app downloads by users under 16, shifting responsibility to app stores and parents. The article frames this as a response to congressional inaction on child online safety, a patchwork of state laws, a 42-state lawsuit, and whistleblower claims. Critics, including the Tech Oversight Project, say Meta is pushing blame onto parents and other companies.
one_line: Meta backs federal legislation requiring parental approval for under-16 app downloads, shifting responsibility to app stores and parents amid lawsuits, whistleblowers and state-law patchwork.
key_facts: Antigone Davis, Meta's global head of Safety, published a blog post on 2023-11-15 supporting federal legislation requiring parental approval for app downloads for users under 16.
Meta cited Pew research showing 81% of U.S. adults favor requiring parental consent for teens to create social media accounts.
A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over harms to teens and young users, partly citing documents from whistleblower Frances Haugen.
Instagram head Adam Mosseri was brought before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record.
A second whistleblower, Arturo Bejar, said Instagram's approach did not protect teens from sexual predators, unwanted advances and harassment.
Congress has not passed online child safety regulation such as KOSA (the Kids Online Safety Act), leaving states to create their own laws.
Utah passed a measure requiring social networks to give parents access to children's posts, messages and comments and to block access during certain hours.
A judge in Arkansas recently blocked a law that would have required parental permission for minors to create social media accounts.
Montana became the first state to ban TikTok, claiming the Chinese Communist Party used it to spy on Americans.
Davis argued that a patchwork of state laws means teens are inconsistently protected as they move between many websites and apps.
Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said Meta would rather push blame onto parents and other companies than design safer products.
Apple and Google did not return requests for comment.
